rubric: PYTHON AS A FIRST LANGUAGE / FUNCTIONAL PROGRAMMING / CHAPTER 28

slides.title: itertools
slides.main: Lazy streams: infinite counters, chaining, grouping, and combinatorics.

slides.title: Infinite streams
slides.main: Always limit an infinite stream: islice, takewhile, or break.

body.text:
from itertools import count, cycle, repeat, islice

print(list(islice(count(10, 5), 4)))
print(list(islice(cycle("ABC"), 7)))
print(list(repeat("x", 3)))
for i, ch in zip(count(1), "abc"):
    print(i, ch)

slides.title: islice
slides.main: The iterator advances: taken and skipped items are used up.

body.text:
from itertools import islice

it = iter(range(100))
print(list(islice(it, 3)))
print(list(islice(it, 2, 5)))       # skip 2, take 3
print(list(islice("abcdefgh", 0, None, 3)))
No negative indexes: an iterator doesn't know its length.

slides.title: chain and zip_longest
slides.sub: Join streams and align different lengths
slides.main: zip drops the longer tail; zip_longest keeps it all.

body.text:
from itertools import chain, zip_longest

print(list(chain([1, 2], (3,), "ab")))
print(list(chain.from_iterable([[1], [2, 3], []])))
print(list(zip([1, 2, 3], "ab")))
print(list(zip_longest([1, 2, 3], "ab", fillvalue="-")))

slides.title: accumulate
slides.main: reduce gives only the total, accumulate gives every step.

body.text:
from itertools import accumulate
import operator

nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]
print(list(accumulate(nums)))
print(list(accumulate(nums, operator.mul)))
print(list(accumulate([3, 1, 4, 1, 5], max)))
print(list(accumulate(nums, initial=100)))

slides.title: Selecting in streams
slides.main: takewhile stops and reads no further, a lifesaver for infinite streams.

body.text:
from itertools import takewhile, dropwhile, filterfalse, compress

nums = [1, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9]
print(list(takewhile(lambda x: x % 2 == 1, nums)))
print(list(dropwhile(lambda x: x % 2 == 1, nums)))
print(list(filterfalse(lambda x: x % 2 == 1, nums)))
print(list(compress("ABCDE", [1, 0, 1, 0, 1])))

slides.title: groupby
slides.main: Sort by the same key first; turn a group into a list at once.

body.text:
from itertools import groupby

words = ["ab", "ac", "ba", "bb", "ad"]
for key, group in groupby(words, key=lambda w: w[0]):
    print(key, list(group))
print("— sorted —")
for key, group in groupby(sorted(words), key=lambda w: w[0]):
    print(key, list(group))

a ['ab', 'ac']
b ['ba', 'bb']
a ['ad']
— sorted —
a ['ab', 'ac', 'ad']
b ['ba', 'bb']

slides.title: Combinatorics
slides.main: Results are lazy: go one by one and stop when you find it.

body.text:
from itertools import product, permutations, combinations

print(list(product("ab", [1, 2])))
print(list(permutations([1, 2, 3], 2)))
print(list(combinations("abc", 2)))
print(len(list(permutations(range(5)))), len(list(combinations(range(5), 2))))

slides.title: starmap, pairwise, tee
slides.main: pairwise is a ready window of two; tee copies an iterator, don't touch the original.

body.text:
from itertools import starmap, pairwise, tee
import operator

print(list(starmap(operator.mul, [(2, 3), (4, 5)])))
print(list(pairwise([1, 2, 4, 7])))
a, b = tee(iter([1, 2, 3]))
print(list(a), list(b))

slides.title: Recipes
slides.sub: From primitives to what you need
slides.main: Many tricky tasks are trivial if you know the right brick.

slides.title: One-line tasks
slides.sub: Pairs, running total, repeats in a row
slides.main: Recognizing the task behind one of these tools is the key skill.

body.text:
from itertools import combinations, accumulate, groupby, islice, count

names = ["Anna", "Boris", "Vera"]
print(list(combinations(names, 2)))
print(list(accumulate([1, -2, 3, -4])))
print("".join(k for k, _ in groupby("aabbcccb")))
print(list(islice((n * n for n in count(1)), 4)))

slides.title: Common mistakes
slides.sub: groupby without sorting and stale groups
slides.main: Limit lazy streams and don't reuse them.

body.text:
from itertools import groupby

data = [1, 2, 1, 1]
print([(k, len(list(g))) for k, g in groupby(data)])   # no sorted: splits up
print([(k, list(g)) for k, g in list(groupby([1, 1, 2]))])   # groups are stale
Also: exhausted tee and permutations, combinatorics size, permutations vs combinations.
